segments.t: Elena has found her car, and it is not in one piece. She stands next to it, assessing the damage while Barinov tries to talk her out of calling the police. Here is the scene in Russian first.
Я в порядке, не я была за рулем.
Да вы не переживайте, я все починю.
если бы вы захотели как хуже.
Let's go through the damage report again, bit by bit.
'Well, the bumper is gone...' 'Bampera net' is literally 'bumper not', and the bumper takes an 'a' ending after 'net'. 'Net' is how Russians say 'there isn't'.
'and the headlight is smashed.' 'Fara' is 'headlight', borrowed from the French word. 'Razbita' is 'smashed', with an 'a' to go with 'fara'.
Я в порядке, не я была за рулем.
'I am fine. I was not driving.' 'V poryadke' is 'in order', so 'fine'. 'Za rulyom' is 'behind the wheel', where 'rul' is wheel. It's the standard phrase for who was driving.
'It is a long story...' The word for 'story' also means 'history', so you could use it for a school subject too. Both words in the phrase end in a feminine ending.
'I will tell you later, okay?' The 'okay' is the little word 'ladno', which Russians use all the time. The first word is 'I will tell', a future.
'All right, bye.' 'Vsyo, davay, poka' is a chain of little words that Russians use to end a phone call. 'Poka' is a casual 'bye'.
Да вы не переживайте, я все починю.
'Do not worry, I will fix everything.' 'Ne perezhivayte' is 'don't worry', in the polite plural. 'Pochinyu' is 'I will fix'.
'I was only trying to help.' 'Khotel kak luchshe' is literally 'wanted as better', and it's a famous Russian phrase for good intentions. People complete it with 'but it turned out as always'.
'I can imagine what you would have done...' The little word 'by' means 'would', and it turns 'what was' into 'what would have been'. Elena uses it to describe a worse version of the day.
если бы вы захотели как хуже.
'if you meant to make things worse.' She plays on his phrase: 'kak khuzhe' is 'as worse', the opposite of his 'kak luchshe'. 'Zakhoteli' is 'you wanted'.
'Do you realize...' 'Voobshche' means 'at all', and 'ponimaete' is 'do you understand', in the polite plural. She leaves the sentence hanging for effect.
'that I could file a complaint?' Russians say 'write a statement' where English says 'file a complaint'. It's the thing you do at a police desk.
'And your chef could go to prison.' 'Posadyat' is literally 'they will seat', and it means 'jail'. The same word means 'sit someone down' and 'plant a tree'.
'I understand.' One word, 'ponimayu'. Barinov is, for once, brief.
'Maybe we can settle this without a complaint?' The word for 'without' makes the next word change its ending, so 'complaint' becomes 'zayavleniya'. 'We'll manage' is a single word.
'I will think about it.' 'Podumayu' is 'I'll think', a polite way of not saying yes. The 'po' at the front means 'for a while'. Now let's listen to the whole conversation again from start to finish.
Я в порядке, не я была за рулем.
Да вы не переживайте, я все починю.
если бы вы захотели как хуже.
Elena says she will think about it, and Barinov looks as nervous as ever. When you watch, notice how little she tells him. Talk soon.
